followUps:
By storing many copies (or coded pieces) of every object in separate failure domains, and by repairing lost pieces fast. Eleven nines is a statistical result, not a promise.

With erasure coding, say 10 data + 4 parity shards spread over different disks, racks and zones, any 4 can vanish and the object is still rebuilt. If a disk fails with probability 1% a year and repair takes hours, losing 5 shards at once is astronomically unlikely. Checksums catch silent corruption and scrubbing jobs rewrite bad shards. Durability is not availability: the data can survive while an outage blocks reads.

Block storage gives raw fixed-size blocks to one machine, file storage gives a shared folder tree, object storage gives whole blobs by key over HTTP.

  • Block (EBS, SAN): low-latency random IO, in-place edits; used for database disks.
  • File (NFS, EFS): hierarchy and POSIX locking, shared by many servers; used for shared home directories.
  • Object (S3): flat namespace, huge scale, cheapest, no partial edits; used for media, backups, data lakes.

Latency order is block, then file, then object; cost per GB is the reverse.

Because objects are immutable: the store replaces a whole object instead of changing bytes inside it. A PUT of the same key writes a new version atomically.

That keeps replication and erasure coding simple, since shards never change in place. To grow a 1 GB log by 1 KB you would rewrite 1 GB. Workarounds: write many small objects (one per minute) and merge later, use multipart upload to assemble a big object from parts, use the copy-with-new-part trick, or choose a store that supports append (Azure append blobs, GCS compose). Streams are usually batched into new objects instead.

Use multipart upload with small parts so a broken connection only costs one part, not the whole file.

A 4 GB file in 16 MB parts is 250 parts. The client uploads 3 to 5 parts in parallel, each with its own pre-signed URL and a retry with backoff. It stores the uploadId and finished part numbers locally, so after a crash it calls ListParts and sends only what is missing. Finally it calls complete with the ordered (partNumber, ETag) list. An abort-incomplete-uploads lifecycle rule (say after 7 days) removes abandoned parts that would otherwise cost storage.

Keep the bucket private and give access only through short-lived, scoped URLs or a CDN that checks a signature.

  • Block public access on the bucket; serve through the CDN with Origin Access Control.
  • Issue signed URLs or signed cookies that expire (for example 10 minutes) and are tied to a key and method.
  • Check ownership in the API before signing.
  • For hotlinking, check the Referer or sign URLs per viewer, and rate-limit by bandwidth.

A leaked signed URL only works until it expires.

Hash the content (SHA-256) on the client or in the worker and use the hash as the storage key, so identical bytes map to one object.

Flow: the client sends the hash before uploading; the API checks a table of hash to key. If it exists, it only adds a new metadata row pointing at the same object and skips the upload. Keep a reference count so deleting one user's photo does not remove the shared bytes. Trade-offs: hashing costs CPU, per-user privacy leaks (a client can learn that a file exists), and you must verify the hash server-side. Dedup saves a lot only for repeated files like memes or shared attachments.

code.title: Multipart upload: parts in any order, ordered complete
code.python:
import hashlib

# Multipart upload model: split, upload parts in any order, complete atomically
data = bytes((i * 7 + i // 256) % 256 for i in range(10240))  # 10,240 byte "file"
PART = 4096                            # part size
store = {}                             # partNumber -> (etag, bytes)

def upload_part(n, chunk):
    etag = hashlib.md5(chunk).hexdigest()
    store[n] = (etag, chunk)           # a failed part can simply be retried
    return etag

parts = [data[i:i + PART] for i in range(0, len(data), PART)]
print("file bytes:", len(data), "parts:", len(parts))
for n in [3, 1, 2]:                    # parallel / out of order is fine
    print("part", n, "etag", upload_part(n, parts[n - 1])[:8])

def complete(manifest):
    # manifest = ordered list of (partNumber, etag); checked before assembly
    out = b""
    for n, etag in manifest:
        assert store[n][0] == etag, "etag mismatch"
        out += store[n][1]
    return out

result = complete([(1, store[1][0]), (2, store[2][0]), (3, store[3][0])])
print("assembled equals original:", result == data)
# Final ETag style: md5 of concatenated part md5s + "-" + part count
combo = hashlib.md5(b"".join(bytes.fromhex(store[n][0]) for n in (1, 2, 3))).hexdigest()
print("final etag:", combo[:8] + "-3")

followUps:
Pick the part size so you stay under 10,000 parts, keep parts reasonably large (8 to 64 MB) to avoid request overhead, and small enough that a retry is cheap.

Minimum is 5 MB (except the last part). For a 100 GB file, 10,000 parts means at least 10 MB each, so 16 MB gives 6,400 parts. Small parts mean more requests and more cost per request; huge parts lose more work on a failure and use more client memory per parallel stream. On a flaky mobile link 5 to 8 MB is common; on a datacenter link 64 to 128 MB.

It is not the MD5 of the whole file. S3 takes the MD5 of each part, concatenates those raw 16-byte digests, takes the MD5 of that, and appends a dash and the part count.

etag = md5(md5(p1) + md5(p2) + md5(p3)) + "-3"

So the same file uploaded with different part sizes gets different ETags. Because of this you cannot use the ETag of a multipart object as a plain content hash; store a SHA-256 yourself or use S3's additional checksums if you need verification.

The last complete call that the store accepts wins, and the object appears atomically; the other caller gets an error or sees the same result depending on timing.

Each uploadId is unique to one initiate call, so two clients normally have different uploadIds and produce two separate objects with the same key, where the later complete overwrites the earlier (unless versioning keeps both). If both use the same uploadId, the first complete succeeds and consumes the upload; the second fails with NoSuchUpload. To stop overwrite races use conditional writes (if-none-match) or unique keys.

code.title: Inverted index and postings-list intersection

followUps:
Store word positions in the postings and check that the positions are consecutive. For "red socks", find docs with both words, then keep those where socks is at position(red)+1.

Example: red is at position 3 in doc 7, socks is at position 4 in doc 7, so doc 7 matches; in doc 9 red is at 3 and socks at 8, so it does not. Positions make the index bigger (often 2x), so engines only store them where phrase search is needed. An alternative for common phrases is indexing word pairs (bigrams) as terms.

Prefix search walks a sorted term dictionary (or trie) to find every term that starts with the prefix; typo tolerance finds terms within a small edit distance.

  • Prefix: binary search the sorted terms for "sock", read until the prefix ends, union their postings. Or index edge n-grams (s, so, soc, sock) for fast autocomplete.
  • Typos: a Levenshtein automaton over the dictionary finds terms within distance 1 or 2; "sokcs" matches "socks" at distance 2. Limit fuzziness to words of 5+ letters.

BM25 is the standard ranking formula: a document scores higher for terms that are rare in the corpus and frequent in the document, but with diminishing returns and length normalisation.

Raw TF-IDF grows without limit: a page repeating "socks" 100 times beats one repeating it 10 times by 10x. BM25 saturates the term frequency (controlled by k1, about 1.2) and penalises long documents (controlled by b, about 0.75). Example: going from 1 to 2 occurrences adds much more score than going from 20 to 21. This resists keyword stuffing and favours short focused documents.

Size shards at roughly 20 to 50 GB each, so 5 TB per day needs about 100 to 250 primary shards per day across the cluster, split over daily or rollover indices.

Steps: estimate on-disk size (raw logs times about 1.1 after compression and replicas multiply it by 2), pick a target of ~30 GB per shard, make the primary count a multiple of your data-node count, and keep under about 20 shards per GB of heap on each node. Use index lifecycle policies: hot (SSD) for 2 days, warm for 2 weeks, cold or searchable snapshots after that, then delete. Test with real queries before committing.

Create a new index with the new mapping, copy the data in, and move an alias to it in one atomic step. Clients always use the alias, so they never notice.

  1. Create products_v2 with the new settings.
  2. Run _reindex from products_v1 (or rebuild from the database) while new writes go to both or are replayed from the stream.
  3. Verify counts, then POST _aliases removing v1 and adding v2 in one request.
  4. Delete v1 after a safety period.

The cluster promotes one of that shard's in-sync replicas to primary, so writes continue after a short pause. Then it rebuilds a new replica elsewhere.

The master node detects the loss (missed pings), picks an in-sync replica (tracked by sequence numbers so no acknowledged write is lost), and the cluster state turns yellow while replicas are missing. If there is no replica the shard is unassigned and the index turns red. With 1 replica you survive one node loss; with replicas on different zones you survive a zone loss. Recovery copies segments and replays the translog.

code.title: Index sync with external versioning and tombstones
code.python:
# Index sync with external versioning: stale or reordered events cannot win
index = {}      # doc_id -> (version, doc) ; deletes stay as tombstones

def apply(event):
    doc_id, version, doc = event["id"], event["v"], event.get("doc")
    current = index.get(doc_id)
    if current is not None and current[0] >= version:
        print("  skip stale", event)          # older/duplicate event is ignored
        return
    index[doc_id] = (version, doc)             # doc None means tombstone

# Events arrive reordered and with a duplicate (version = DB row version)
events = [
    {"id": 1, "v": 1, "doc": "red socks"},
    {"id": 1, "v": 3, "doc": "red wool socks"},
    {"id": 1, "v": 2, "doc": "red cotton socks"},   # late: must lose to v3
    {"id": 2, "v": 1, "doc": "blue hat"},
    {"id": 2, "v": 2, "doc": None},                 # delete
    {"id": 2, "v": 1, "doc": "blue hat"},           # replayed old event
    {"id": 1, "v": 3, "doc": "red wool socks"},     # duplicate delivery
]
for e in events:
    print("apply", e)
    apply(e)
print("final index:", index)

followUps:
Nothing is lost: the events wait in the log, and the indexer catches up when it restarts. Search is just stale for an hour.

Kafka retains the events and the consumer group remembers its committed offset. After restart the indexer reads from that offset in large bulk batches. Because indexing uses versions, replaying duplicates is harmless. You need log retention longer than the worst outage (for example 7 days), alerting on consumer lag, and enough indexer throughput to drain faster than new data arrives. If retention was exceeded, do a full reindex from the database.

Make the index change backward compatible when possible, otherwise build a new index version and swap an alias. Never edit a field's type in place.

Adding a new field is easy: update the mapping, deploy the indexer that fills it, and backfill old documents with an update-by-query. Changing a type or analyzer requires a new index: create v2, reindex from the database (the source of truth), run the indexer into both v1 and v2 briefly, and then flip the alias. Keep a schema version in the document so the indexer and search code can handle both during rollout.

Send all events for one document id to the same Kafka partition by using the id as the message key. A partition keeps order and one consumer reads it.

Kafka orders messages only within a partition, so key = document id gives per-document order. With CDC (Debezium) the key is the primary key. Add a version column, such as the row version or the log sequence number, and use external versioning in the index as a safety net against retries and rebalances. You do not need global order, only per-document order.

Gorilla stores the first timestamp in full and then only the change of the change, and stores each value as an XOR with the previous one, using almost no bits when things are regular.

Timestamps every 10 s: deltas are 10, 10, 10, so delta-of-delta is 0 and costs a single bit. Values: if a gauge stays 21.5, XOR with the previous value is 0, one bit again. When a value changes slightly, only the few differing bits are stored. Result: about 1.37 bytes per point instead of 16. It works because metrics are regular and change slowly.

Store a mergeable summary, never the percentile itself, because percentiles of percentiles are wrong.

If one 5-minute bucket has p99 of 200 ms and another 400 ms, the hourly p99 is not 300 ms. Use histograms with fixed buckets (Prometheus style) or sketches like t-digest or DDSketch: each rollup holds a small sketch, and sketches from many buckets can be merged and then queried for any percentile with a small error (about 1%). Keep raw only for a short time.

Prometheus suits pull-based monitoring and alerting with a single node and short retention; InfluxDB is a purpose-built push TSDB; TimescaleDB is PostgreSQL with time partitioning.

  • Prometheus: PromQL, service discovery, alerting; local storage, scale out with Thanos or Mimir.
  • InfluxDB: high write rates, built-in retention, flexible tags.
  • TimescaleDB: full SQL, joins with business tables, continuous aggregates.

I pick Prometheus for infra metrics, Timescale when I need SQL and joins.

code.title: Rollups that merge exactly: count, min, max, sum
code.python:
import random
random.seed(7)
# Raw points: one sensor, one reading every 10 s for 1 hour
raw = [(t, 20 + random.random() * 5) for t in range(0, 3600, 10)]
print("raw points:", len(raw))

def rollup(points, bucket):
    # Keep count, min, max, sum: they merge exactly, avg = sum / count
    out = {}
    for t, v in points:
        b = t - t % bucket
        c = out.setdefault(b, [0, v, v, 0.0])
        c[0] += 1; c[1] = min(c[1], v); c[2] = max(c[2], v); c[3] += v
    return out

five = rollup(raw, 300)
print("5-minute buckets:", len(five))
# Hourly rollup built from the 5-minute ones (mergeable, no raw data needed)
cnt = sum(c[0] for c in five.values())
lo = min(c[1] for c in five.values())
hi = max(c[2] for c in five.values())
tot = sum(c[3] for c in five.values())
print("hour count=%d min=%.2f max=%.2f avg=%.2f" % (cnt, lo, hi, tot / cnt))
print("direct avg=%.2f" % (sum(v for _, v in raw) / len(raw)))
print("storage: %d raw -> %d rollups" % (len(raw), len(five)))
# Averaging averages would be wrong when counts differ; sum+count is safe.

followUps:
Keep it only for the sensors and window that need it, and store everything else downsampled, because uniform 1-second data costs 10 times the raw 10-second volume.

1M sensors at 1 s is 1M points/s, 86 B/day, about 120 GB compressed per day, so a year is about 44 TB per customer-share if all sensors are included. Charge or scope it: only that customer's sensors, tiered storage (SSD for 7 days, object storage in Parquet after), and dashboards that read rollups unless the user zooms in. Agree the cost with the customer first.

Alert on silence: for every sensor track the last time it reported and fire when now minus last_seen is bigger than a few reporting intervals.

Sensors report every 10 s, so a threshold of 60 s (6 missed readings) avoids flapping. A stream job keeps last_seen per sensor in state; a timer fires per sensor, or a periodic query lists sensors with a stale timestamp. Group alerts by gateway or site: if 5,000 sensors on one gateway go quiet at once the problem is the gateway, not the sensors. An absent series is invisible to normal threshold alerts, so this needs explicit design.

Shard by sensor id (hash) so one sensor's data stays together, and partition by time inside each shard so retention is a cheap drop.

Ingest is 100k points/s; with each node good for about 20k to 50k/s you need 4 to 8 nodes plus replicas. Hash(sensor_id) % N gives even load. Queries for one sensor hit one shard; fleet-wide aggregates fan out and merge, which is why rollups matter. Use consistent hashing or many small virtual shards so adding nodes moves little data. Time partitions per day make dropping data a metadata operation.

ETL transforms data before loading it into the warehouse; ELT loads raw data first and transforms it inside the warehouse or lake with SQL.

ETL made sense when warehouse compute was scarce; it needs a separate transformation server and loses raw detail. ELT is now common because cloud warehouses scale compute cheaply: land raw data (bronze), run dbt models for cleaned (silver) and business tables (gold), and rerun when logic changes since the raw copy is kept. ETL is still right when you must remove sensitive data before it lands.

A star schema has one central fact table of events with numbers, surrounded by small dimension tables that describe them.

Example for sales: fact_sales(date_key, product_key, store_key, quantity, amount) with dimensions dim_date, dim_product, dim_store. Choose the grain first (one row per order line). Facts hold measures and foreign keys; dimensions hold descriptive text you filter and group by. Queries join the fact to a few dimensions and aggregate, which engines optimise well. Slowly changing dimensions (type 2 rows with valid-from and valid-to) keep history.

You need a table format that supports row-level deletes (Iceberg, Delta, Hudi), because plain Parquet files cannot be edited in place.

Steps: find the user's rows through an index or key (keep a user-id column or a catalogue), run DELETE WHERE user_id = X, which rewrites the affected files or writes delete files, then run compaction and expire old snapshots so the deleted data really leaves storage, including time-travel history. Also purge backups within the legal deadline (30 days). Better still: key or encrypt per user and delete the key (crypto-shredding).

It means the query engine skips partitions (folders) that cannot match the filter, so it never reads those files.

If data is laid out as events/date=2025-03-01/, events/date=2025-03-02/ and so on, then WHERE date = '2025-03-02' reads one folder out of 365, about 0.3% of the data. It works only when the filter is on the partition column in a plain form. Do not partition on a high-cardinality column like user_id (millions of tiny folders); daily or hourly is typical.

Too many tiny files make queries slow, because each file costs a listing, an open, a footer read and a task. The fix is to compact them into files of about 128 MB to 1 GB.

It happens with streaming writes every few seconds or over-partitioning: 100,000 files of 100 KB is 10 GB but takes far longer to scan than 20 files of 500 MB. Fix by writing larger batches, using a scheduled compaction job (Iceberg rewrite_data_files, Delta OPTIMIZE) and choosing coarser partitions.

Parquet and ORC are columnar and best for analytics; Avro is row-based and best for streaming and record-by-record writes with a schema.

  • Parquet: columnar, broad support (Spark, Trino, warehouses), the default for lakes.
  • ORC: columnar, strong in the Hive world, built-in indexes and ACID support.
  • Avro: row-based, compact, supports schema evolution; used in Kafka messages and landing zones.

Rule of thumb: Avro to move data, Parquet to query it.

code.title: Word count with a combiner and hash shuffle
code.python:
from collections import defaultdict
lines = ["the cat and the dog", "the cat sat on the mat", "the dog ran"]
R = 2   # number of reducers
print("input:", lines)

def mapper(line):
    return [(w, 1) for w in line.split()]

def combine(pairs):
    # Combiner: pre-sum locally so fewer pairs cross the network
    c = defaultdict(int)
    for w, n in pairs:
        c[w] += n
    return list(c.items())

# Map phase (one mapper per line) and shuffle by hash(word) % R
shuffled = [defaultdict(list) for _ in range(R)]
total_raw = total_combined = 0
for line in lines:
    pairs = mapper(line)
    comb = combine(pairs)
    total_raw += len(pairs); total_combined += len(comb)
    for w, n in comb:
        r = sum(map(ord, w)) % R         # stable hash for a repeatable demo
        shuffled[r][w].append(n)
print("pairs shuffled without combiner:", total_raw, "with:", total_combined)

# Reduce phase: each reducer sees all values for its keys
for r in range(R):
    out = {w: sum(v) for w, v in sorted(shuffled[r].items())}
    print("reducer", r, out)

followUps:
A combiner is a small reducer that runs on each mapper's output before the shuffle, so less data crosses the network. It is safe only when the operation is associative and commutative.

Word count: a mapper that saw "the" 5 times sends (the, 5) instead of five (the, 1) pairs. Sum, max, min and count are safe. Average is not: avg(avg(1,2), 3) = 2.25 but the true average of 1,2,3 is 2. Make it safe by combining (sum, count) pairs and dividing at the end. The framework may run a combiner zero, one or several times, so the result must not depend on it.

Spark keeps data in memory between steps and plans the whole job as a graph, instead of writing to disk after every map and reduce.

An iterative job with 10 passes over data in MapReduce does 10 disk write-read cycles; Spark caches the dataset once in RAM, often 10x or more faster. It offers richer operators (join, groupBy, window) instead of only map and reduce, SQL and DataFrames with an optimizer, and streaming and ML libraries. Lost partitions are recomputed from lineage rather than re-read from replicated disk.

Count words in each partition, keep a small heap of the K biggest, then merge the heaps. You never sort all words.

  1. Job 1: word count (map, combine, reduce).
  2. Each reducer keeps a min-heap of size K of its (count, word) pairs: O(n log K).
  3. Send the R small heaps to one machine and merge them: R x K items.

Because each word lives on exactly one reducer, the global top K is within the union of local top K lists. For huge key sets use count-min sketch plus a heap for an approximation.

A stage is a group of tasks that can run without moving data between machines. Spark cuts a new stage at every shuffle (wide dependency).

Narrow steps like map, filter and select run together in one stage, pipelined over each partition. groupBy, join (without broadcast) and repartition need data from all partitions, so the stage ends and the next one starts after the shuffle. Example: read, filter, map (stage 1), reduceByKey (shuffle), map, write (stage 2). The Spark UI shows stages, and fewer shuffles means fewer stages and a faster job.

AQE lets Spark change the plan while the job runs, using real statistics from finished stages instead of guesses.

  • Coalesces many tiny shuffle partitions into fewer, so 200 default partitions of 1 MB become 5 sensible ones.
  • Switches a sort-merge join to a broadcast join when one side turns out to be small after filtering.
  • Splits skewed partitions so one giant key is handled by several tasks.

It is on by default in recent Spark versions and is usually a free win.

Do not use Spark when the data fits on one machine or when you need low-latency answers per request.

For a few GB, pandas, DuckDB or a single SQL database finishes in seconds without cluster startup (often 30 to 60 s) and cost. For sub-second serving use a database or search index. For true record-at-a-time low-latency streaming, Flink or Kafka Streams fits better. If the job is a simple SQL transform inside a warehouse, run it there instead of moving data out.

code.title: Event-time windows, watermark and late events
code.python:
# Tumbling 10 s windows, event time, watermark = max event time - 5 s lateness
WINDOW, LATENESS = 10, 5
counts = {}              # window start -> count
emitted = set()
max_ts = 0
# (event_time, arrival order is the list order): some arrive out of order
events = [1, 4, 12, 8, 15, 3, 21, 18, 26, 9]
print("events (event time in arrival order):", events)
for ts in events:
    start = ts - ts % WINDOW
    if start in emitted:
        print("event", ts, "LATE: window", start, "already emitted, dropped")
    else:
        counts[start] = counts.get(start, 0) + 1
    max_ts = max(max_ts, ts)
    watermark = max_ts - LATENESS            # engine's estimate of event-time progress
    for s in sorted(counts):
        if s + WINDOW <= watermark and s not in emitted:
            emitted.add(s)
            print("watermark", watermark, "-> emit window [%d,%d) count=%d" % (s, s + WINDOW, counts[s]))
print("never emitted (still open):", {s: c for s, c in counts.items() if s not in emitted})

followUps:
A tumbling window is a fixed block of time that does not overlap; a session window groups events from one user's burst of activity and closes after a gap with no events.

Tumbling 10 minutes: every event falls in exactly one slot (12:00 to 12:10, 12:10 to 12:20). Session window with a 30 minute gap: clicks at 12:00, 12:05 and 12:20 form one session; a click at 13:10 starts another. Session sizes vary per user and windows can merge when a late event bridges two sessions, so they need more state and care.

Measure the real delay of your data and choose a bound that covers most events, usually the 99th or 99.9th percentile of lateness, then send the rest to a side output.

If 99% of events arrive within 3 seconds and 99.9% within 20 seconds, a 20 s bound is a reasonable start. Each extra second delays every result by a second and keeps more window state. For billing choose a long bound or reconcile in batch; for dashboards a short one is fine, and the late tail is corrected later. Monitor the count of dropped late events.

If you replay with event time and the same logic, you get the same results, because results depend on the timestamps in the events and not on the wall clock.

Processing-time windows give different answers each replay because the data arrives faster. With event time, a replay of old data runs quickly, and the watermark advances by the data's own timestamps. Watch out for sinks: use idempotent upserts or transactions so the replay overwrites rather than double counts, and for sources with late data decide whether to use the original lateness settings.

Unaligned checkpoints let barriers jump ahead of queued data, so a checkpoint completes quickly even when the job is under heavy backpressure.

Normally an operator with several inputs waits until the barrier arrives on all of them (alignment), and under backpressure that wait can take minutes. In unaligned mode the operator takes the snapshot at once and also stores the in-flight buffers it skipped over as part of the state. Checkpoints finish fast but are bigger, because they hold buffered records, so use them only when alignment time is a problem.

Take a savepoint, stop the job, and start it again with a different parallelism. Flink redistributes the state across the new tasks.

Keyed state is split into key groups (the max parallelism, default 128 or more when set), and each task owns a range of key groups. Going from 4 to 8 tasks means each task takes half the groups. Set max parallelism large enough up front because it cannot be changed without losing state, and give operators stable uids so state maps correctly after code changes.

Flink is a true record-at-a-time streaming engine with low latency; Spark Structured Streaming processes small micro-batches, though it also has a continuous mode.

  • Flink: latency in milliseconds, rich state and timers, strong event-time control, two-phase commit sinks.
  • Spark: latency of about 100 ms to seconds, same API as batch DataFrames, simpler if the team already uses Spark.

I choose Flink for stateful, low-latency work, Spark when batch and streaming code reuse matters most.

Cut the data at a clear boundary, such as a day, and make each side own one side of it: batch owns closed days, streaming owns the open day. Then the final value replaces the provisional one, never adds to it.

Example: billing for 2025-03-01 comes only from the batch table once the partition is sealed (after the lateness window). Streaming shows today's running total, written by key (customer, window), and the serving view takes batch if it exists, else streaming. Never sum the two. Idempotent writes keyed by window make replays safe.

Migrate in steps: first land the raw events in a lake, then reimplement the logic once on the stream engine, run it side by side, compare, and only then switch and retire the old code.

  1. Keep the old lambda running; add raw event storage in Iceberg.
  2. Write the shared logic as one Flink SQL job in streaming and bounded modes.
  3. Run both pipelines and compare results daily; fix differences.
  4. Move dashboards, then billing, to the new tables; delete the old batch code.

Plain batch is enough whenever results that are hours old are acceptable, which is more often than people think.

Daily finance reports, monthly invoices, model training, and nightly dashboards need no streaming. Batch is simpler to build, test and rerun; it costs less since machines run only for the job; and exactness is easy because the input is fixed. Add streaming only when a clear business case, like fraud checks or live alerts, needs seconds-level results.

Use micro-batches or incremental refresh every 5 minutes on your existing warehouse, not a full streaming stack.

A scheduled job (or dbt incremental model) every 5 minutes reads only new rows since the last watermark, for example WHERE updated_at > last_run, and merges them. Or use warehouse features such as dynamic tables or materialized views with a 5-minute target lag. This avoids cluster management, state and checkpoints, and a failed run is simply rerun. Cost is a small compute burst every 5 minutes.

Test them with deterministic input and event-time timestamps, so the same input always gives the same output, and check results at the end of the data rather than at a wall-clock time.

  • Unit-test the pure logic (parsing, windows) with fixed events.
  • Use the engine's test harness or a bounded input with explicit watermarks, including late and out-of-order events.
  • Test recovery: kill the job mid-run, restart from a checkpoint, and assert the output has no loss or duplicates.
  • Compare against a batch run over the same data.

Say it plainly: the fast number is an early estimate, and the final number arrives later and is the one that counts.

For example: "Today's revenue on the dashboard is live and may move by about 0.5% as late events arrive; the figure on tomorrow morning's invoice is final." Label values in the UI as Provisional or Final, show the time they were last updated, and publish the typical gap (say under 1%). Never bill from provisional data. Agreeing this up front prevents disputes about changing numbers.
